contents.name: Section 2.4: constants of motion, dF/dt = 0 along Lagrange solutions, the theorem that dL/dt = 0 implies H = sum qdot_j p_j - L is constant, and the cyclic-coordinate claim p_j = ∂L/∂qdot_j constant
Section 2.4.1: continuous symmetry of the Lagrangian and the proof of Noether's theorem producing the conserved quantity sum_i (∂L/∂qdot_i)(∂Q_i/∂s)|_{s=0}
Section 2.4.1 Example 'Homogeneity of Space': translation invariance of the closed system and conservation of the total linear momentum (2.56)-(2.57)
Section 2.4.1 Example 'Isotropy of Space': rotational invariance and conservation of the component n . L of the total angular momentum (2.58)-(2.60)
Section 2.4.1 Example 'Homogeneity of Time': conservation of H for a Lagrangian with no explicit time dependence, identified with the total energy for the systems considered
Remark after Section 2.4.1 that 'all conservation laws in nature are related to symmetries', including electric charge and baryon number
contents.reason: Rhetorical universal claim with no proof and no converse; the page asserts only the conditional deductions and explicitly declines any converse, so the remark is not used.

contents.name: Section 2.5 applications (bead on a rotating hoop, double pendulum, two-body reduction, Lagrange points)
contents.reason: Applications of the formalism to constrained and central models; they belong to the earlier CM04-CM06 pages and to later CM09/CM15 pairs, not to the symmetry page.

sources.title: K. K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Part CM: Classical Mechanics (title page last edited September 1, 2026), 252-page main volume

contents.name: Section 2.3 'Hamiltonian function and energy': generalized momentum (2.31), the Hamiltonian function (2.32), dH/dt = -∂L/∂t (2.35) and H = const for ∂L/∂t = 0 (2.36)
Section 2.3: the rotating-ring example where the Hamiltonian differs from the mechanical energy, E - H = mR^2 omega^2 sin^2 theta, while H is conserved (2.40)-(2.41)

Section 2.4 'Other conservation laws': cyclic coordinate implies ∂L/∂q_j = 0 and p_j constant (2.48), the footnote naming the Noether theorem as the general statement, and the central-force example p_phi = mr^2 phidot = L_z (2.49)-(2.54)
Section 2.5: exercise problems (pendula, bead on a hoop, rod on a cylinder)
contents.reason: Exercise statements without worked solutions; the framework does not promote unsolved exercises into proved claims, and their content concerns earlier one-dimensional and constrained-model pages.

contents.name: Section 1.8.1-1.8.2: momentum state functions, cyclic coordinates and Dp_i = 0 along realizable paths, with the warning that momenta depend on the chosen Lagrangian

Section 1.8.5: Noether's theorem for a parametric coordinate transformation, the invariance condition L-tilde(s) = L, and the Noether integral I = (∂_2 L)(DF-tilde(0)), with the central-potential rotation example giving (minus) the angular momentum
Section 5.4.4: point transformations and the rotating-coordinate example in which the Hamiltonians differ by the product of the angular momentum with the angular velocity of the coordinate system
Section 5.4.5: addition of a total time derivative to the Lagrangian, the momentum shift ∂_1 G and the Hamiltonian shift -∂_0 G
Section 1.8.3-1.8.4: central forces in three dimensions and the restricted three-body problem
contents.reason: Central-force mechanics belongs to the CM05 pair and the restricted three-body problem to later specialised models; the page needs only the Noether mechanism, which is harvested above.
